Where these belong

This whole file is intended for a private repository, so everything in it can be committed together.

If you ever make that repository public, only four of these belong in it — sentinel-blue.pyz, README.md, LICENSE and SHA256SUMS. The source, the patch and the evidence are your private tree, and the bundled public README.md states that source and evidence are kept privately. Publishing this file as-is would contradict that line and expose the full source and tests.

How to run it

sentinel-blue.pyz is a Python zipapp. You run it — you do not open it or unzip it. If your system says "this file type cannot be opened", that is expected; it is not a file you double-click.

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS            # expect: sentinel-blue.pyz: OK
python3 sentinel-blue.pyz --version
python3 sentinel-blue.pyz doctor   # reports anything missing
python3 sentinel-blue.pyz desktop  # the operator window

On Windows use py sentinel-blue.pyz --version. On Linux you can also chmod +x sentinel-blue.pyz and run ./sentinel-blue.pyz --version.

Requires Python 3.11 or newer with cryptography. SSH/WinRM deployment also needs paramiko, smbprotocol and pyspnego; the desktop window needs Tk.

If you want a copy that needs no Python at all, that is the offline bundle — a separate artifact that ships its own CPython and every dependency, launched with ./Start-Sentinel-Blue.sh. The newest one built is 1.9.74, which predates every fix here. It can be brought up to date without an internet connection and without rebuilding Python:

sh python3 tools/repack_offline_bundle.py \ --previous "sentinel-blue-1.9.74-offline-linux-x86_64.zip" \ --runtime sentinel-blue.pyz \ --output ./repacked

It verifies every checksum in the old bundle before touching it and refuses if anything was tampered with. Your bundled Python and wheels carry over untouched.

Rebuild and re-verify

mkdir source && tar xzf sentinel-blue-1.9.78-source.tar.gz -C source && cd source
PYTHONPATH=src:tests python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t tests -q   # expect 778 OK
PYTHONPATH=. python3 tools/build_defensive_release.py --output ../build
sha256sum ../build/sentinel-blue-1.9.78.pyz     # must equal dcde16b1...

The build is reproducible — building twice from the same tree gives the same digest. That is how you confirm the runtime in this file came from this source.

python3 tools/controlled_continuity_acceptance.py --runtime ../build/sentinel-blue-1.9.78.pyz --output ../cont.json
SENTINEL_LEDGER_DIR=/tmp/lg1 python3 tools/smoke_release.py --exercise-lifecycle --exercise-crash-resume ../build/sentinel-blue-1.9.78.pyz
SENTINEL_LEDGER_DIR=/tmp/lg2 PYTHONPATH=src python3 tools/smoke_release.py --exercise-supervisor ../build/sentinel-blue-1.9.78.pyz
PYTHONPATH=src python3 tools/packaged_withdrawal_check.py ../build/sentinel-blue-1.9.78.pyz

--exercise-supervisor cannot be combined with --exercise-lifecycle; they are separate fault fixtures and the harness refuses the combination on purpose.

Commit to your private repository

Save this file out of your browser and commit it, optionally alongside the extracted files:

cd /path/to/Sentinel-Blue
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
git add -A && git commit -m "1.9.78: boot upgrade, offline policy skew, payload inventory, collection cost, Linux persistence response, service fault diagnosis, measured host capacity and visible backup stalls"
git push origin main && git tag -a v1.9.78 -m "Sentinel Blue 1.9.78" && git push origin v1.9.78

GitHub renders a committed .html file as source text rather than as a web page, so to read it you download it and open it locally. The file is self-contained, so a local copy needs no network.

Versioning

Each round of fixes takes the next patch number — 1.9.78, 1.9.79, … through 1.9.99, then 2.0. 1.9.76 was the issue-#13 round, 1.9.77 added measured host capacity, and 1.9.78 makes a stalled recovery backup visible.

This series is numbered above 1.9.75 because it carries 33 changes the published 1.9.75 does not. One version number should not mean two different artifacts depending on when someone pulled it.

A bump touches five files, and the build tool refuses to build if they disagree:

File What it holds
pyproject.toml version = "…" — the source of truth the build tool reads
src/sentinel_blue/__init__.py __version__ — must match, or the build refuses
README.md first line must be # Sentinel Blue <version>
examples/inventory.example.json the example inventory's pinned version
public release notes the ## Release notes: <version> heading

One version string is never bumped. MINIMUM_POLICY_SCHEMA_VERSIONS = {1: '1.9.74', 2: '1.9.75'} in offline_continuity.py records the release in which each offline-policy schema first shipped — it is history, not a current version. Schema 2 really did ship in 1.9.75 (verified against the published runtime). Moving that entry would make the controller refuse offline authority to perfectly correct 1.9.75 agents. A blind find-and-replace across the tree will break it; check it after every bump.

Historical references such as docs/RECOVERY_CONTINUITY_1.9.74.md and the example URLs in examples/inventory.example.json name the release they describe and are also left alone.

Fixes in this build

All P0, P1 and P3 issues are fixed, along with the fixable P2 items. The patches apply to the published 1.9.75 source; the reconstructed tree rebuilds byte-identically to 8f3ac7ce…, so they are against exactly what is on GitHub.

Why 1.9.78. This build carries 33 changes the published 1.9.75 does not, so shipping it as 1.9.75 would have given one version number two different meanings depending on when someone pulled it. The published 1.9.75 keeps its number and its digest. 1.9.76 was the issue-#13 round, 1.9.77 added measured host capacity, and 1.9.78 makes a stalled recovery backup visible. Each further round takes the next patch number — 1.9.79, 1.9.80 — through 1.9.99, and then 2.0.

One version string is deliberately not bumped: MINIMUM_POLICY_SCHEMA_VERSIONS = {1: '1.9.74', 2: '1.9.75'} records the release in which each offline-policy schema first shipped. Schema 2 really did ship in 1.9.75 (verified against the published runtime), and moving that entry would make the controller refuse offline authority to correct 1.9.75 agents.

P0

  1. Boot registration survives an upgrade. --ledger-directory is optional and honored as absent only for a pre-pinning (schema 1) registration, which uses the default ledger exactly as before. Legacy bindings are compared on the schema they were reviewed under, so they cannot authorize a ledger they never covered. Newer registrations still require their exact pinned ledger; unknown schemas are refused; Withdraw still blocks boot.
  2. Offline policy version skew. The controller refuses to issue offline authority to an agent whose release cannot parse the policy, naming that agent and the required release, and still accepts a policy signed under the older schema.
  3. 32 MiB fingerprint ceiling. A new streaming RestorePointStore._hash_target fingerprints running executables up to the existing 512 MiB Windows ceiling under the same aggregate budget, retaining no bytes, with the same symlink, race and stability gates. Restoration and quarantine keep their smaller limits.
  4. Baseline blocked by ordinary upgrades. Payload coverage gaps now carry the typed provenance the collector serializes and are reported as warnings that cost score, while real collector failures still block.
  5. Hidden refusal reasons. rejection_error shows the controller's own reason, stripped of non-printable characters and capped at 200 characters, and keeps the generic message when there is no usable reason.

P1

  1. Controller-identity conflict is explained once instead of an identical warning every second, and names the only safe resolutions.
  2. A service without health says why: the manifest host is not an enrolled agent, the agent is disabled, telemetry is missing or stale, or no matching service check ran. The desktop shows these under the Services summary.
  3. Setup review runs the execution-time provisioning gate, so a plan that execution would refuse can no longer be approved first.
  4. Alerts carry a severity column, sorted most severe first and colored.
  5. A retained message log on the Session tab keeps errors that previously vanished from the footer one at a time.
  6. Offline authorization names the missing baseline item instead of "missing or ambiguous".

P2

  1. Native Windows acceptance for the new WinRM receipt and ACL paths — not fixable here; it needs a Windows host.
  2. Windows ledger entry cap — left as documented risk; changing it needs Windows testing.
  3. Supervisor smoke test fixed, and it exposed a real finding. The fixture used the machine-wide mutation ledger, so another Sentinel process or a stale lock on the same host silently blocked the scheduled backup the check waits for. Each fixture now gets its own ledger, controller output goes to a private file instead of an undrained pipe (which could block every controller thread once the buffer filled), and the check accepts capsule backups. All three smoke modes pass.
  4. The review window now leads with severity, type, host, summary and recommended action, and explains what each button does.
  5. Configuration errors print a reason and exit 2 instead of a traceback.

P3

17–19. LICENSE, a public README.md and SHA256SUMS are prepared in the sentinel-release/ folder for the repository. 20. Offline bundles are still unpublished — that is your decision, and the Windows bundle cannot be rebuilt here. 21. Readable backup names are back (sentinel-blue-<UTC stamp>-b<sequence>-<id>) and are shorter than the 1.9.75 names, so the Windows path guard still holds. Pruning continues to order by the signed sequence in the manifest.

Issue #22 — collection pressure delays recovery

Measured first: with 303 MB of running service binaries, collection spent 1.67 s of every cycle re-hashing bytes that never changed, on the agent's 15-second loop. A slow or stale collection is what blocks automatic recovery, which is the substance of issue #22.

  • Fingerprint cache. A payload fingerprint is reused only while the file's device, inode, size, mode, owner, group, modification time and inode-change time all match the previous observation. An in-place rewrite, a replacement, a metadata change, or a restored modification time all miss the cache.
  • Bounded staleness. Every cached entry is re-read within 15 minutes regardless, at most four per pass so expiry cannot produce one very expensive cycle, and an out-of-range age in either direction (a backwards clock) re-reads.
  • Restoration, quarantine and integrity capture never consult the cache.
  • Replaced running binaries are now inventoried. When a process's executable has been swapped, /proc/<pid>/exe points at the deleted inode, so the new file at that path was never fingerprinted at all. It is now, and the missing running image is still reported as a coverage gap.

Measured result (303 MB of running service binaries, same host, same load):

Result
Fingerprint pass, previous behaviour 1.67 s median, repeated every cycle
Fingerprint pass, with the cache 0.35 s median
Whole cycle, previous behaviour 0.57 s sustained, 2 coverage gaps every cycle
Whole cycle, with the cache 0.20 s sustained, 1 gap, converging
Large service binaries actually fingerprinted 2 of 3 forever → 3 of 3 from cycle 2

The coverage numbers matter more than the timings. Without the cache the payload budget is spent re-reading the same bytes, so one large service binary was never fingerprinted at all — it could have been swapped with no fingerprint change to notice. With the cache, coverage converges to complete and stays there. A binary swapped by rename with its timestamps restored was detected either way.

Collection pressure is now visible

collection_seconds rides along with each observation, and the controller raises a collection_pressure alert: medium past 15 s (slower than the agent's own interval, so observations fall behind) and high past 45 s (half the freshness window, where recovery risks acting on stale evidence or being held). An older agent that does not send the field is unaffected, and a malformed value never drops the sample.

tools/measure_collection_pressure.py now times the Linux collector sections as well as the Windows ones, reports the agent's own measure, the payload cache hit/miss/revalidation counts and coverage gaps, and fails a run whose collection is slower than a budget you can set with --collection-budget-seconds. That is the harness to run in your lab for the "representative event load" evidence #22 needs.

Issue #16 (Linux) — revoking one cron entry

A cron line is standard red-team persistence, and it was the one common Linux technique with no safe response. /etc/crontab is on the critical list, so removing it wholesale was correctly refused — but that left no way to remove just the attacker's line from a file that also holds legitimate and teammate jobs.

  • New cron-entry target, mirroring the proven SSH-key revocation: the exact reviewed line is identified by its SHA-256 and removed; every comment, environment assignment, whitespace detail and other job in the file is kept byte for byte. Repeated identical lines are all removed and counted.
  • Only schedule lines are targets. Comments, blank lines and environment assignments (SHELL=, PATH=) can never be revoked, and the five-field and @reboot-style forms are both recognized.
  • Locations are allowlisted: /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/*, /var/spool/cron/* and /var/spool/cron/crontabs/*. Anything else — including /etc/passwd, sshd_config and /etc/cron.daily/ scripts, which are whole files and remain ordinary file targets — is refused.
  • security scan now lists each crontab's revocable entries and digests, so a reviewer can pick the exact line. This is in the scan result only; telemetry keeps its existing shape, so there is no version-skew risk.
  • Removal keeps the existing guarantees: refused if the file changed after review, uncertainty recorded before any write, evidence preserved, replay safe, and restore puts the original file back byte for byte.

Verified end-to-end on a real /etc/cron.d file, and again through the packaged runtime: the malicious entry was revoked, the teammate job and SHELL= line survived, and restore reproduced the original file exactly.

Note: this area had no test coverage at all before — the remediator was untested. The 15 new tests cover parsing, the allowlist, refusals and the remove/restore round trip.

Issue #16 (Linux) — timer, socket and path unit persistence

A .timer, .socket or .path unit starts its payload without ever being a .service, and only .service names passed validation. Such a unit could be handled as an ordinary file target, which deleted the unit file while systemd still held the loaded, enabled unit.

  • New systemd-unit target for .timer, .socket and .path units. It is stopped and disabled natively, then its file is removed, then the daemon is reloaded — the same order a service unit already used. restore re-enables and restarts it exactly as before.
  • The existing systemd-service target is untouched, so reviewed service targets keep their exact meaning; .service is refused under the new kind.
  • Unsafe unit names (traversal, shell metacharacters, newlines, unsupported unit types) are refused.
  • Quarantine is confirmed only when systemd agrees the unit is gone; if it still holds the unit, the operation is recorded uncertain for review rather than reported as clean.

Timer units were already inventoried, so detection existed — only the response was missing. The native sequence is asserted against a stub, since this sandbox has no systemd; the systemd calls themselves still need your lab, like every other native path.

Issue #15 (Linux) — sudoers privilege persistence

A drop-in such as /etc/sudoers.d/99-backdoor granting NOPASSWD:ALL is one of the cheapest ways to keep root. It was invisible: /etc/sudoers.d/* appeared in neither the startup inventory nor the default protected paths, so neither a new drop-in nor an edit to an existing one produced any observation.

  • Detection. Drop-ins are now inventoried as sudoers persistence items and are default protected paths, so a new or modified drop-in is both an unverified-persistence observation and an integrity change. /etc/sudoers itself was already protected.
  • Bounded response. A new sudoers-entry target revokes one reviewed grant by its digest, keeping Defaults, aliases, @includedir, comments and every other grant byte for byte. Aliases, includes and Defaults lines can never be targeted.
  • No self-lockout. A grant to root, %sudo, %wheel, %admin or ALL is refused with "held for human review" — before any write. Removing administrator access is a human decision, not an automatic one.
  • security scan lists each sudoers file's grants, each with its digest, principal and an administrator_grant flag, so a reviewer sees immediately which lines are safe to revoke.
  • Remove and restore keep the existing guarantees, including file mode (0440 in the round-trip test).

A caveat worth stating: the revocation is byte-level, not a visudo syntax check. Removing one grant from a valid policy leaves a valid policy, but a visudo -c verification step would be a sensible addition on a real host.

Issue #13 (Linux) — a service that is down now says why, and a hopeless restart is not attempted

This is the "unknown fault" item. When a scored service went down, diagnosis produced exactly one word — service_stopped — and recovery proposed a restart. The information needed to do better was already in every observation and simply discarded: the agent collects systemd's Result=, ExecMainStatus=, SubState= and NRestarts= for every unit, and every listening port with its owning process. None of it reached diagnose_service.

Two consequences, both of which cost points in a real round:

  1. A unit systemd was refusing to start (past its start-rate limit) looked identical to one that had simply been stopped. Recovery restarted it, systemd refused, the attempt budget drained, and the operator saw "recovery attempted, service still down" with no reason.
  2. A service whose port an attacker's listener had taken over could never come back, and nothing said so.

What was added

  • The service manager's verdict is now named. Nine Result= values map to named causes: a start-rate limit, an out-of-memory kill, host resource exhaustion, an exit status, a signal or core dump, a start timeout, a watchdog expiry and a startup-contract violation. A verdict this release does not recognize is reported as native_failure_reason_unrecognized rather than silently dropped — an unknown fault stays visibly unknown.
  • exit-code with status 0 is read correctly. systemd records that when the main process succeeded but the unit's type contract was never met. Calling it an application error would send an operator to the wrong place, so it is a startup-contract fault.
  • A restart loop is recognized as one. auto-restart is an activating state, so a flapping service previously produced native_state_unknown — an unknown fault in the most literal sense. It is now named, from the sub-state and, where an approved baseline makes the number meaningful, a restart counter climbing by three or more.
  • A declared port held by another process is detected. Ports come from the service's own loopback transactions (an explicit port, or an http(s) URL); an unstated port is never guessed, because a guess turns an unrelated listener into a false accusation. Only TCP listeners on loopback or the wildcard count — a listener bound to a different address does not block this bind.
  • Socket activation is not mistaken for a hijack. A .socket unit legitimately holds the port while its service is inactive. That is recognized (the holder is PID 1), reported separately, and does not block recovery.
  • A running unit is never given a stale cause. Result= keeps the last failure until the unit starts again, so it is not reported as a current fault.

Where the line is drawn

Five causes mean a restart cannot succeed: a start-rate limit, an out-of-memory kill, host resource exhaustion, a loop systemd is already driving, and an occupied port. Recovery and coordinated repair both refuse these and state the reason, instead of spending the attempt budget. Everything else — a plain crash, a signal, a start timeout, a watchdog expiry, a startup-contract violation — is still restarted automatically, because a restart is the right answer to a program that crashed once. No new automatic action was added; this only ever adds evidence or withholds a mutation, consistent with issue #18.

The refusal is now raised before the less specific state checks, so a flapping unit is told "the service manager is already restarting this unit in a loop" rather than "recovery requires an explicitly stopped approved running service".

What the operator sees

The Services table's reason column now names the cause on a stopped row instead of leaving it blank — "it was killed for host memory", "another process holds its declared port (8080)". A cause that blocks a restart outranks one that does not, since a single line should say why the service will stay down. The recovery report adds the cause as a hypothesis with its domain (service_control, host_capacity, port_conflict) and the discriminating check to run next.

Verified end-to-end through the shipping controller ingest path, with a real process holding the port — see sentinel-work/issue13-fault-scenarios.txt:

Scenario Restart queued What the operator is told
Program crashed once (exit-code, status 1) yes it exited with an error status (1)
systemd refusing to start (start-limit-hit) no the service manager is refusing to start it past its restart limit
Out-of-memory kill (oom-kill) no it was killed for host memory
Unit already cycling (auto-restart) no the service manager is restarting it in a loop
Foreign process holding the declared port no another process holds its declared port (18085)
Socket-activation unit holding the port yes it exited with an error status (1)

Linux only, as you asked. Windows service exit codes are not mapped, and the port correlation uses the same telemetry on both platforms but is untested on Windows. A systemctl reset-failed step for the start-limit case is deliberately not automated — clearing a failure state is a reviewed action, not a reflex.

Host capacity (Linux) — measured, not inferred

This finishes what #13 started. #13 could name an out-of-memory kill only because systemd happened to record one. A filesystem with no room stops a service just as reliably and leaves no such verdict: the service simply fails to write, and recovery restarts it into the same wall until its attempt budget is gone. A full /var is one of the most common ways a scored service dies in a competition — log floods, a crash-dump, an attacker deliberately filling the disk — and the agent had never once looked.

What is collected

Free space, free inodes, read-only state and memory headroom, from statvfs and /proc/meminfo. Nothing is derived from command output. Three details worth stating:

  • Free space excludes the root reserve. f_bfree counts blocks only root may use; an ordinary service sees f_bavail. Reporting the larger number would overstate headroom precisely when it matters. There is a test asserting this.
  • One row per device, not per path. /, /var and /tmp are usually one filesystem; reporting it three times would triple every alert about it.
  • Bounded and never fatal. At most 16 filesystems; a mount point that will not answer is skipped and the rest are still reported.

Alerts

host_capacity_low at 10% free (medium) and 3% (high), separately for space and for inodes; host_memory_pressure on the same thresholds.

Inodes are checked separately from bytes on purpose. A filesystem can be 90% empty and unable to create a single file. This was reproduced on a real 12 MB ext4 volume: 90.4% of the space free, 0 of 64 inodes free, every open() failing with ENOSPC. A bytes-only check reports that volume as healthy.

A large volume also no longer cries wolf: 5% of a 4 TB disk is 200 GB, so an absolute floor of 8 GiB free suppresses the percentage alert.

Recovery

A service whose own declared files or data sit on a filesystem that is full, out of inodes, or read-only gets a named finding and its restart is held — a service that cannot write cannot start. Only the filesystems under that service's required_files and required_data are considered, matched by longest mount point, so a full volume elsewhere on the host is never blamed for it. The hold thresholds (1% and 16 MiB) are deliberately tighter than the alert thresholds: warn early, refuse late.

This also applies to a service that is running. A running service on a full filesystem is failing, even though it is up.

The boundary that matters

Capacity that was never reported is unknown, and unknown is never healthy. An older agent sends no capacity at all; the field stays absent rather than defaulting. A default of "0 bytes free" would hold recovery on every 1.9.76 agent; a default of "plenty" would hide a real fault. Absent means absent, and an older agent still recovers normally. There are tests for both directions.

Impossible values are treated as unknown rather than trusted: free above total, or available memory above total memory, zeroes the pair.

Verified against a real filesystem

Not synthetic numbers — a 12 MB ext4 volume mounted, filled for real, measured by the agent's own collector, and run through the shipping controller ingest path (sentinel-work/host-capacity-scenarios.txt):

Scenario Measured Restart queued What the operator is told
Filesystem with room 11,345,920 B free (90.4%) yes —
Filesystem really full 0 B free (0.0%) no the filesystem holding its files is full
Space reclaimed 11,345,920 B free (90.4%) yes —
Inodes exhausted 90.4% space free, 0/64 inodes no the filesystem holding its files is out of inodes

The third row matters as much as the second: the hold is not sticky. Clear the disk and recovery resumes on the next observation with no operator action.

Windows collects no capacity yet — the fields are absent there, which the controller reads as unknown. That is the honest state, not a silent zero.

Ledger contention and stalled backups — a silent stall becomes visible

This is the loose end from P2-14. Fixing the supervisor smoke test turned up a real condition: a second Sentinel process on the same host shares the machine-wide mutation ledger, and whoever loses the race blocks. The wait itself was already bounded at 60 s. Two other things were wrong, and both mattered more.

The error blamed the wrong thing

Every lock timeout produced the same sentence, whatever the cause:

A mutation is still active; withdrawal has not drained this host

That is an assertion the code could not support. An operator reading it goes and investigates Withdraw, which has nothing to do with a contended lock. The message now states what is actually known and names the process holding it:

The mutation ledger at /var/lib/sentinel-blue-ledger stayed locked for 60s; process 1967 on web-01 has held it for 60s. Either another Sentinel process on this host is using the same ledger, or a mutation has not drained. Give each process its own SENTINEL_LEDGER_DIR, or pause and drain this host.

The holder writes its PID, host and start time into the lock file for the next waiter. That record is advisory only — it names a process for a person to look at and is never trusted for a decision. It is bounded to 512 bytes, and a truncated, tampered or absent record degrades to "the holding process did not identify itself" rather than raising or inventing a holder.

A wait longer than 5 seconds is also logged while it is still only a wait, so contention that eventually succeeds is still visible instead of appearing as an unexplained pause.

The failure that mattered reached nobody

When the blocked caller was the scheduled recovery backup, LOG.exception was the whole response. Nothing on the dashboard, no alert. During an event nobody reads controller logs, so recovery capsules are assumed to exist right up until the moment they are needed and are not there. That is the worst shape a failure can take in this system.

Scheduled backup health is now first-class:

  • controller.recovery_backups on the dashboard carries last success, last attempt, consecutive failures, the bounded reason, and the ledger contention counters.
  • A high-severity recovery_backup_failing alert is raised once backups are both overdue (two missed intervals) and have failed twice running. One slow cycle or a briefly contended ledger is ordinary and raises nothing.
  • The alert fires once per failure run, not once per cycle, and re-arms after a success — so a genuine outage is impossible to miss and a flapping one does not bury the board.
  • It is attributed to a reserved sentinel-controller identity, so an alert about the controller itself cannot be attributed to, or spoofed by, an enrolled host.

The monitor must not be able to cause what it reports

A monitor for a silent stall that can itself stall the maintenance loop would reintroduce the fault it exists to report. Both new calls are housekeeping, not core steps: they are guarded, a raising monitor cannot withhold the maintenance heartbeat or skip pruning, and a raising recorder cannot make a successful backup look failed. An older app object without the methods still maintains normally.

Verified with two real processes

Not a stubbed lock — a second process holding the ledger through spawn (sentinel-work/ledger-contention-scenario.txt). 29 tests cover the holder record (including a tampered one), the bounded wait, the warning, the alert lifecycle, and the guarantee that the monitor cannot break the loop.

One of those tests caught a defect in my own fix: a lock file containing a JSON array raised AttributeError, which was outside the exception types I was catching. The code was fixed, not the test.

Verification

  • Full suite: 778 tests, 0 failures (555 original + 223 new).
  • Focused exact-runtime acceptance: 44/44 on the final build.
  • All three smoke modes pass, including the previously failing supervisor mode.
  • Packaged withdrawal fixture behaves as before: Remove completes, Restore & Withdraw is held pending outside verification.
  • Live on one VM: agent enrolled, service healthy, stopped service detected as critical within seconds; the desktop showed the severity column, the real refusal reason, and the retained message log.
  • One test caught a bug in my own P0-5 fix (a non-string error field would have been formatted into the message); the code was fixed rather than the test.

What is still open on #22

  • Windows still re-reads every cycle. The cache is wired into the POSIX path only; the Windows branch is unchanged and untested here.
  • Startup and protected-file reads are uncached — measured at 0.002 s for 20 config files, so not worth the added risk today.
  • The load validation #22 actually asks for needs a real host: systemd, journald, real services, representative event load. The harness is ready; the lab is yours.
  • The cache is per-process, so an agent restart pays the cold cost once.

Before you ship

  • The rebuilt runtime is dcde16b16f3f88f8830f95a022de9da69266604f7288b10a6e9a246f76a5b79a. Update release.sha256 in every event profile and re-run your packaging checks.
  • Upgrade controller and agents together where you can.
  • Still worth adding: a controller-boot-uninstall / rebind command, and a bounded wait with a logged warning when the mutation ledger lock is contended (the silent block found in P2-14).

Public release notes

This is the README that ships in the public repository, reproduced in full.

A portable Blue Team defensive control platform for authorized Windows and Linux competition and practice networks. It monitors hosts and scored services, raises alerts, records evidence, and — within explicitly approved limits — restarts declared services and restores approved files. Every high-impact change is scope-checked, validated against the real service, and reversible; anything unknown is held for a person.

This repository contains one file: the portable runtime sentinel-blue.pyz. Source, tests, evidence and operating documents are kept privately.

Requirements

  • Python 3.11 or newer with cryptography; SSH/WinRM deployment also needs paramiko, smbprotocol and pyspnego, and the desktop window needs Tk.
  • Linux: x86_64, glibc 2.34+, systemd, iproute2, plus an X11/XWayland session for the window.
  • Windows: x64, Windows Server 2022 is the acceptance target.
  • No internet connection, cloud account or AI service is needed to run it.

Verify before running

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
python3 sentinel-blue.pyz --version
python3 sentinel-blue.pyz doctor

The checksum in SHA256SUMS is the same value your event profile pins in release.sha256.

Quick start

python3 sentinel-blue.pyz desktop      # operator window
python3 sentinel-blue.pyz controller --help
python3 sentinel-blue.pyz agent --help
python3 sentinel-blue.pyz observer --config observer.json

A controller needs a reviewed event profile, private token files, a recovery key and anchor, and TLS material. Agents enroll to it with a derived one-time ticket. The desktop's tabs cover session recording, service health, alerts and verification, credentials, setup, Withdraw and Recovery.

What it does and does not do

Does: local and external service checks; native collection of processes, services, accounts, listeners, startup items and file integrity; bounded restarts of declared services; restoration of approved files; setup and rollback for systemd services, nginx, Linux IPv4 routing, Windows services, firewall allow rules and IIS; durable, tamper-evident action history; emergency Pause, Remove and Restore & Withdraw; portable session recordings.

Does not: attack back or touch anything outside the authorized scope; scan undeclared systems; install software or run arbitrary setup scripts without review; rotate credentials blindly; act on unknown outcomes; or claim a host with root or SYSTEM compromise can be proven clean. Automatic behavior is off unless the event profile approves it.

Release notes: 1.9.78

Fixes in this build, all relative to 1.9.75:

  • Upgrades no longer break controller-boot registration. A registration written by an earlier release still starts; newer registrations keep their exact pinned ledger.
  • Offline restart authorization across releases. The controller refuses to hand offline authority to an agent that cannot use it and names the required release; policies signed by an older controller are still accepted.
  • Large and updated programs no longer break inventory. Running executables are fingerprinted by streaming, so a program over the old 32 MiB limit, or one replaced by a package update, no longer blocks baseline approval and automatic recovery.
  • The desktop explains refusals instead of showing only an HTTP status, ranks alerts by severity, keeps a message history, and explains what Approve, Observe and Reject do.
  • Setup review refuses plans that execution would refuse, rather than failing after approval.
  • Clearer messages for a service with no health data, an approved baseline missing a required item, a host pinned to a different controller, and configuration errors on the command line.
  • Readable recovery backup names are back, while paths stay short enough for Windows.
  • Collection no longer re-reads unchanged programs every cycle (issue #22). A fingerprint is reused only while a file's exact identity is unchanged, and every entry is re-read on a rotating schedule, so a slow collection no longer delays recovery. Measured on a host with 303 MB of running service binaries: the fingerprint pass fell from 1.67 s to 0.35 s median, sustained cycle cost from 0.57 s to 0.20 s, and payload coverage went from 2 of 3 large binaries (permanently incomplete) to 3 of 3.
  • Collection pressure is now reported. Each observation carries how long it took, and the controller raises an alert when collection falls behind its own interval or approaches the freshness window, instead of recovery quietly running on stale evidence.
  • Sudoers drop-ins are now watched, and a single grant can be revoked. /etc/sudoers.d/* is inventoried and protected; one reviewed grant can be removed while the rest of the policy is preserved, and grants carrying administrator access (root, %sudo, %wheel, %admin, ALL) are held for human review instead.
  • Timer, socket and path units can now be quarantined. These start a payload without being a service; they are stopped and disabled through systemd before the unit file is removed, and restored the same way.
  • A single cron entry can now be revoked from a shared crontab. A malicious schedule line is removed by its exact digest while every other job, comment and environment line in the file is preserved, and it can be restored exactly. security scan lists each crontab's entries and digests.
  • A replaced service binary is now fingerprinted. Previously, swapping a running program's file left the new file uninventoried, because the process still pointed at the deleted original; the missing running image is still reported as well.
  • A down service now says why it is down, and a hopeless restart is no longer attempted (issue #13). The service manager's own verdict — a start-rate limit, an out-of-memory kill, an exhausted host, a restart loop, an exit status, a signal, a start timeout, a watchdog — is read from every observation and named, and so is a declared listening port held by another process. Five of those causes mean a restart cannot succeed: recovery holds and states the reason instead of spending its attempt budget, while a program that simply crashed is still restarted automatically. A legitimate socket-activation unit holding the port is recognized and does not block recovery. Linux only for now; Windows service exit codes are not yet mapped.
  • Host capacity is now measured, not inferred. Each observation carries free space, free inodes and memory headroom for the filesystems a service depends on, and the controller raises a graded alert before they run out. A service whose own filesystem is full, out of inodes, or mounted read-only is named as such and its restart is held, because a service that cannot write cannot start. Inode exhaustion is reported separately from a full disk: a volume can be 90% empty and still unable to create a single file. A very large volume with tens of gigabytes free no longer alerts on percentage alone. An agent that reports no capacity is treated as unknown, never as healthy. Linux only.
  • A stalled recovery backup is now visible instead of silent. Scheduled backup health — last success, consecutive failures and the reason — is on the dashboard, and a high-severity alert is raised once backups stop succeeding, rather than the failure reaching only a log file nobody reads during an event. A contended mutation ledger, the most common cause, now names the process holding it and says which setting fixes it, instead of asserting that withdrawal had not drained the host. A long wait is warned about while it is still only a wait.

Still open: native Windows, reboot, multi-host and live SSH/WinRM acceptance; broad application, identity and cross-host recovery; measured detection quality. Unknown outcomes and unapproved changes are held for an operator by design.

One Linux VM: setup guide

Everything runs on one Ubuntu or Debian VM over 127.0.0.1.

Note. This guide was written against the 1.9.74 offline bundle, which is still the most recent offline bundle built. The flow is unchanged. Troubleshooting entries that no longer apply are marked inline.

Everything runs on one Ubuntu or Debian x86_64 VM and talks over 127.0.0.1. This flow was tested with the 1.9.74 script: the agent enrolled, services were checked, and a stopped web service raised a critical alert about 4 seconds later.

Before you start

  • OS: x86_64 Linux with glibc 2.34 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04+ or Debian 12+), systemd, and iproute2 (ip, ss).
  • Desktop: a graphical session (X11 or XWayland), needed only for the GUI.
  • VM state: a fresh VM, or a snapshot taken before Sentinel was ever run on it (see Troubleshooting).
  • Files: the complete Linux offline ZIP (sentinel-blue-1.9.74-offline-linux-x86_64.zip), including its runtime/ folder.

1. Extract and check the bundle

mkdir -p ~/sentinel && cd ~/sentinel
unzip /path/to/sentinel-blue-1.9.74-offline-linux-x86_64.zip
cd "Sentinel Blue 1.9.74 linux-x86_64"      # the folder name inside the ZIP
chmod -R u+X runtime; chmod u+x runtime/bin/python* Start-Sentinel-Blue.sh
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS | grep -v ': OK' # prints nothing if every file is intact
./Start-Sentinel-Blue.sh offline-check --desktop

2. Generate the configuration

Copy prepare-single-vm.py into the bundle folder. Then list the services you want watched, in the form NAME:PORT:http or NAME:PORT:tcp:

runtime/bin/python3 -I prepare-single-vm.py --bundle . --out ~/sentinel-private \
  --service web:80:http --service ssh:22:tcp

This creates ~/sentinel-private (owner-only permissions) containing:

  • the secrets
  • a TLS certificate
  • an approved event profile
  • the service-check configuration
  • the recovery anchor
  • the agent's one-time enrollment ticket
  • three start scripts

3. Start everything (three terminals)

~/sentinel-private/start-controller.sh        # terminal 1: leave running
sudo ~/sentinel-private/start-agent.sh        # terminal 2: root gives full visibility
~/sentinel-private/start-desktop.sh           # terminal 3: opens the window

The agent should print completed first enrollment. After that, it logs only warnings.

4. Connect the desktop

On the Connection tab, enter these values (start-desktop.sh prints them too):

Field Value
Controller https://127.0.0.1:8765
Operator identity operator
Credential epoch 2
Controller CA certificate ~/sentinel-private/controller.crt
Signing key Load signing key file, then ~/sentinel-private/operator.key

Then press Connect.

5. Use it

  • Services: local health and checks passed. Stop a service and it turns unhealthy within seconds.
  • Alerts & verification: a popup announces new items. Select one, press Review selected request, then choose Approve, Observe or Reject. On a fresh VM, expect medium alerts for login-capable accounts and a high alert for your sudo user. Mark the ones you recognize as legitimate.
  • Baseline: approve Review initial baseline. Automatic recovery can't work without it. The controller refuses if collection has errors; see Troubleshooting.
  • Session: press Start to record. At the end, press Stop & save and keep the ZIP.
  • Pause automatic changes (Services tab) is the emergency brake.

Troubleshooting

  • The agent logs continuity path unavailable ... HTTP 400 over and over.
  • Cause: this VM's agent already trusted a different controller. The trust is stored in /var/lib/sentinel-blue-ledger, which is a safety feature.
  • Fix: keep using the original ~/sentinel-private, or start from a fresh VM or snapshot.
  • Don't delete the ledger to get around this; the project's rules forbid erasing it.
  • The GUI says "HTTP 403; refresh and review the current state."
  • FIXED IN 1.9.78. The desktop now shows the controller's own reason for a refusal. If you still see the bare status, you are running an older build.
  • Cause: a safety rule refused the request.
  • Most common reasons:
    • The agent is stopped or stale.
    • Baseline approval requires error-free collection and healthy service checks.
  • Baseline approval keeps failing. Check whether any of these applies:
  • A service check is failing.
  • ip/ss or systemd are missing.
  • ~~A running program is larger than 32 MiB~~ — FIXED IN 1.9.78. Large binaries are fingerprinted by streaming, up to 512 MiB.
  • ~~A running program was replaced by an update.~~ — FIXED IN 1.9.78. A replaced running binary is inventoried at its path, and the missing running image is reported as a coverage gap rather than blocking approval.
  • Payload coverage gaps no longer block baseline approval at all; they are warnings.
  • New in 1.9.78: if the filesystem holding the service's files is full, out of inodes, or read-only, the Services table now says so directly.
  • A service shows unknown. The agent isn't running, or the service wasn't generated by prepare-single-vm.py. A service's host must be the agent ID, and each check needs a matching entry in probes.json.
  • The runtime won't start. Keep runtime/, launch.py, offline-manifest.json and sentinel-blue.pyz together, and don't edit the .pyz. Its checksum is pinned in the profile.

Limits of this setup

  • Practice use only. It's a loopback setup for learning and rehearsal. For a real event, use the event's addresses, identities and approved profile.
  • Setup tab: it only applies systemd services and nginx here. It won't install packages or run custom scripts.
  • Not auto-started: nothing starts at boot unless you use Recovery → Enable controller at boot, which hasn't been tested on real machines in 1.9.74.

Separately, inodes were exhausted on the same volume while 90.4% of its space was still free — 0 of 64 inodes, every open() failing with ENOSPC. That produced service_filesystem_inodes_exhausted and a high-severity alert. A check that looked only at bytes would have reported that volume as healthy.

Ledger contention — before and after

Two real processes, one machine-wide ledger — the exact condition that silently blocked scheduled backups:

Scenario: a second Sentinel process on this host shares the machine-wide ledger
          (the exact condition that silently blocked scheduled backups)

  holder identity recorded in the lock file:
    process 2906 on vm has held it for 0s

  a scheduled backup waiting on this ledger now fails in 2.0s with:

    The mutation ledger at /tmp/sentinel-contention-e2e-uydlh9y8/sentinel-blue-ledger stayed locked for 2s; process 2906 on vm has held it for 2s
    Either another Sentinel process on this host is using the same ledger, or a mutation has not drained
    Give each process its own SENTINEL_LEDGER_DIR, or pause and drain this host.

  BEFORE this fix the same condition produced:
    A mutation is still active; withdrawal has not drained this host
    ...and nothing on the dashboard, no alert, only a line in the controller log.

  contention counters for this process: {'warnings': 0, 'timeouts': 1}
  after the other process released, the lock is acquired normally; counters: {'warnings': 0, 'timeouts': 1}

Still open

Needs a lab, not more code.

  1. Native acceptance on real VMs. Every fix here is Linux-verified only. Windows especially: the WinRM receipt and ACL paths have never run on Windows.
  2. #12 application coverage (BIND/DNS, MySQL/MariaDB, Postfix, vsftpd) — the biggest competition-scoring gain, but it needs those services installed.
  3. Offline bundle is still 1.9.74. It can be repacked to 1.9.78 offline with the command shown above; the Windows half needs a Windows host.
  4. Windows host capacity. Linux now measures free space, inodes and memory; Windows reports none, which the controller reads as unknown.
  5. Windows ledger entry cap — left as a documented risk; changing it needs Windows testing.
  6. controller-boot-uninstall / rebind command so a boot registration can be replaced without hand-editing systemd or Task Scheduler.
  7. Ledger lock contention — a contended machine-wide ledger silently blocks scheduled backups. A bounded wait with a logged warning would make the stall visible.
  8. #30 detection quality — needs a red team.

Worth remembering

  • The agent pins the first controller it meets in the machine-wide ledger (/var/lib/sentinel-blue-ledger); a second generated setup on the same VM is refused. Use a fresh VM or snapshot, or set SENTINEL_LEDGER_DIR for test fixtures. Do not delete the ledger to get around this.
  • Payload coverage gaps are warnings rather than baseline blockers, but they are still reported — do not let them pile up unread.
  • Clearing a systemd failure state (systemctl reset-failed) is deliberately not automated. #13 detects the start-rate limit and holds; unblocking it stays a reviewed human action.
  • A capacity hold is not sticky. Clear the disk and recovery resumes on the next observation with no operator action.
  • apt and PyPI are blocked in the build sandbox, as are non-HTTP ports, so Proxmox and Azure testing has to run from your own machine.
